utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the Registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-02-54-R77.4, the contempt proceeding against Mr. Kosta Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the appearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of the Respondent this morning, Stephane Bourgon, counsel from Montreal, Canada, accompanied by Ms. Jesenka Residovic as interpreter and legal assistant. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And pursuant to Rule 77, this matter is being prosecuted by the Chamber. When the Chamber last met to consider this matter some two weeks ago, we adjourned to give time to Mr. Bulatovic to consider the matter and to take advice. I am now going to put the charge to Mr. Bulatovic, who will respond guilty or not guilty. Normally you would stand, Mr. Bulatovic, but I see that you are not well, so you may sit. Kosta Bulatovic, born in 1937 in the village of Dobrusa in northern Metohija, is charged that on 19 and 20 April 2005, being a witness before Trial Chamber III of the International Tribunal, he knowingly and wilfully interfered with the administration of justice by contumaciously refusing to answer questions asked by the Prosecution contrary to Rule 77(A)(i) of the Rules. How do you plead to that, Mr. Bulatovic; guilty or not guilty? THE RESPONDENT: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit. The factual foundation for the charge is set out in the transcript for the 19th, pages 38591 to 38595, and on the 20th at page 38616, and those pages clearly show that on both occasions it was explained to Mr. Bulatovic that by refusing to answer questions put to him by the Prosecutor in cross-examination, he was exposing himself to a charge of contempt. On both occasions, Mr. Bulatovic declined to answer. The second occasion he stated that he was maintaining his position. That's the factual foundation for the case. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, with your leave this morning, before the presentation of the case for the Defence of Mr. Bulatovic, there are some issues that I would like to raise with the Trial Chamber. The first such issue, Mr. President, is related to the rescheduling order, which was issued by the Trial Chamber on the 4th of May. Pursuant to this order, the Trial Chamber rescheduled the proceedings against Mr. Bulatovic until this morning, and the order states that this was at the request of counsel for the Respondent because of difficulties in preparing to defend against the charge of contempt which were engendered by the lack of certainty regarding the legal representation of the Respondent. Mr. President, I'm not quite aware of the discussions which led to this order being issued, and I don't want to make this situation more difficult than it really is, but nevertheless, I would like to state for the record that when this order was issued, I was not assigned to represent Mr. Bulatovic, and I did not request this adjournment. More importantly, I would like to avoid causing any prejudice to Mr. Bulatovic, to the Respondent, on the basis of this alleged uncertainty concerning his legal representation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me say immediately that no prejudice, no question of prejudice could arise. No question of prejudice could arise at all. Nothing turns on this, Mr. Bourgon. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. President. The next issue I would like to raise concerns the notice concerning the presentation of the case for the Defence, which I filed on behalf of Mr. Bulatovic yesterday, on the 5th of May. At paragraph 4 of this notice, I stated that the Defence was considering whether to present a preliminary motion in relation to a potential witness with whom the Defence was not able to meet. First, I would like to confirm that of course the words "preliminary motion" in this paragraph did not refer to a preliminary motion pursuant to Rule 72, and I'm quite certain that the Trial Chamber picked that up and understood that what I meant really was an application which I wanted to make before the commencement of the case for the Defence pursuant to Rule 73, and I apologise for this mistake. Nevertheless, Mr. President, the problem encountered with this potential witness is indeed very real. Without going into too many details at this time, I would simply like to say that this witness is a staff member of the International Tribunal whom I was not permitted to meet on the basis that this witness is immune from the legal process pursuant to the United Nations Convention on the Privileges and Immunities, and that only the Secretary-General of the United Nations was able to consent or to waive this person's immunity and allow the person's testimony. Now, what is important here is that this person, this witness, had a conversation with the Respondent concerning the conditions of his testimony before the Trial Chamber in this case, and I am of the view that this witness may offer evidence which is likely to be of assistance to the Trial Chamber in adjudicating on the contempt issues against the Respondent. For this reason, Mr. President, I'm still considering whether to make this application, and I will get back to this issue at a later stage in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're familiar with Article 30 of the Statute.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness falls within what section of that article? Is it paragraph 3, which relates to the staff of the Prosecutor and the Registrar enjoying the privileges and immunities accorded to officials of the United Nations under Articles 5 and 6 of the 1946 Convention?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I am aware of this provision, Mr. President, and I don't wish to enter into the specific topic at this time. However, there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm raising it because it may be that I can determine the issue if I have enough information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge, I did not hear what you said, if you were addressing me. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wasn't addressing you, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I was asking if you have -- if you have information about the person, too, because if the person doesn't qualify, then the issue doesn't arise at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, in this particular case, I was contacted by a representative of the Registrar of the International Tribunal, telling me that the position of the Registrar was that this person was covered by this convention. Now, whether I agree or not is the subject of my application if and when I make it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. What I understand you to be saying is that once we've heard the rest of the case, you may decide to seek an adjournment because you want to lead another witness. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In part. In part, Your Honour, you're right, but not exactly, because I need to get into my next issue, and my next issue will determine whether I need to seek -- to see this witness or not. But maybe there's a way to avoid having to seek an adjournment to hear this witness, and that's why I'd like to get leave from the Trial Chamber to get into my next issue, which I believe is a much more important issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. But I'll just tell you that it is the -- in my view, it's the Court, it's the Chamber which is the final arbiter of the -- of questions like this under Article 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. May I, with your permission, proceed with the next issue, and then we can come back to this one later on? I just wanted to make -- to make it clear that what I was referring to when I filed my notice with respect to the presentation of the case for the Defence, and provide the Trial Chamber with what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The next issue I'd like to raise at this time, having spent some time preparing for this case, I have come to the conclusion that it is necessary for me to present an oral preliminary motion pursuant to Rule 72, challenging the jurisdiction of the Trial Chamber to adjudicate on these contempt proceedings. And before I do so, I would like to provide the Trial Chamber with my respectful submissions and the rationale for making such an application at this time. First, Mr. President, as the Trial Chamber will remember, on the 20th of April, I made an application for the Trial Chamber to request that these proceedings be transferred to another Chamber, a request which was denied by a majority decision. On the 27th of April, I also filed a motion requesting certification of this decision with a view to filing an interlocutory appeal, which was also denied on the 3rd of May, 2005. I note carefully, Mr. President, that in its decision denying my request for certification, the Trial Chamber stated that the legal issues discussed in my application of 27 April were beyond the scope of the limited proceedings against the Respondent. Accordingly, I will not attempt to raise those issues de novo. However, there remains one issue which I had some difficulty coming to terms with. In my view, Mr. President, I respectfully submit that the Trial Chamber erred in law when it decided to continue the testimony of the Respondent in the absence of the accused Milosevic, and I cannot avoid the conclusion that without this alleged error of law by the Trial Chamber, my client would never have been the object of contempt proceedings and he would not be here this morning. Accordingly, Mr. President, there must be a way for my client to obtain redress of this situation before the Trial Chamber proceeds with the contempt charges. It then occurred to me that there were two choices, or two possible options, which I then reduced to only one on the following basis: The relevant question I put to myself was the following: Is it a defence for the Respondent to say that he was not in contempt of Court because the Trial Chamber erred in law in going ahead with his testimony in the absence of the accused Milosevic? If the answer to this question is yes, then redress can be obtained by the Respondent as part of the contempt proceedings. If the answer to this question is no, then if this is not a defence which is open to the Respondent in these proceedings, then redress must be obtained elsewhere. Having considered the matter and reviewed the transcript of the hearing held on 20 April, and having sought the advice of other Defence counsel, because I must admit I was looking for what the real answer should be, I concluded that, in my view, it was not a defence, because the Trial Chamber did make a ruling on the issue, namely that it could proceed with the testimony of the Respondent in the absence of the accused Milosevic and that it could not review its own decision. Consequently, the only way for the Respondent to seek redress of this situation before the commencement of the contempt proceedings would be to challenge the jurisdiction of the Trial Chamber on the following basis: One, if the Trial Chamber erred, it implied that it could not proceed with the testimony of the Respondent. Two, if it could not proceed with the testimony of the Respondent, then its order on contempt of 20 April is ultra vires of its inherent powers. And three, if the contempt order of 20 April is indeed ultra vires of the inherent powers of the Trial Chamber, then this Trial Chamber does not have jurisdiction to proceed with the contempt proceedings. In light of the above, Mr. President, this is the application I would like to make at this time; namely, to challenge the jurisdiction of the Trial Chamber pursuant to Rule 72, a preliminary motion with the exact words "preliminary motions" underlined, on the basis of an error of law. With your leave, Mr. President, I would proceed to make this application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand the submission. You've conceded that the Trial Chamber can't review its own decision, and therefore you have no redress by that route, and then you say if the Trial Chamber erred, it implies it could not proceed with the testimony of the Respondent; if it could not proceed with the testimony, then its order is ultra vires. That's you going back again to the question of whether the decision to proceed with the testimony was correct or not. So you're back to the same question again. Now, this sounds like gobbledegook to me. Can you clarify it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. This is exactly the type of questions I was playing around with not only last night but discussing with other counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is futile, Mr. Bourgon, when the issue of whether or not it was right to proceed with the trial is one for the Appeals Chamber, if this ever gets to the Appeals Chamber. It's beyond us now to make that decision, to reverse that decision. We made it, and it's over. And the question then is whether the witness was bound to answer the questions put. And indeed it may even be that if we were wrong in that, it may even be - I don't know the answer to this at the moment, it will have to be resolved elsewhere if it arises - but it may even be that even if we were wrong, he was still bound to answer the questions. That that's how courts ought to be respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I may respond, Your Honour. There is a difference, in my view, between the Respondent having to go through contempt proceedings, being found either guilty or not guilty, or whether the initial findings of contempt are vacated or not and then going to the Appeals Chamber to seek redress of that decision, of that ruling, and the Respondent seeking before, before this proceeding, whether there should have been contempt proceedings in the first place. Now, what you highlight, Your Honour, is exactly the point I wish to raise. I respectfully submit that the Trial Chamber did not have jurisdiction to issue that order because there was an error of law in its decision to continue. If, as Your Honour says, the Trial Chamber is not able to continue with its -- to reverse its own decision or to review, then it must go to the Appeals Chamber because it's a matter of jurisdiction at this stage and not after the proceedings when a ruling has been made by the Trial Chamber, because it is an issue of jurisdiction, and pursuant to Rule 72, there is an appeal as of right, and that's the difference. Now, in my respectful submission, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But at the end of the process is the appeal of right. This is so we get the job done, that we don't spend all our time going round in circles like this, retreading the same ground several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to come back on this issue, but the -- there is a difference here, because the complete issue of these proceedings, these contempt proceedings, the underlying issue, that was my first submission I made when I first addressed Your Honours on the 20th of April, is that there is a direct link between that decision of the Trial Chamber and the contempt proceedings. If that decision is erroneous, there should not be contempt proceedings. That's a way different from vacating a finding of contempt after such proceedings. Now, in my respectful submission, Your Honour, I believe that this issue, the best way to address this, and there is ample discussion in the transcript of the 19th of April, whereas all the parties in the courtroom, namely court assigned counsel, counsel for the Prosecution, and again in my respectful submission the Trial Chamber, agreed that there was an issue here, and the issue is: Does this decision from the Appeals Chamber allow us to do this? And there was a consensus that detailed submissions would be required in order to arrive at a decision. I believe that the best way to proceed in such a case would be for the parties in the real trial, the trial of Mr. Milosevic, to take this issue, to make their detailed submissions, and after that, once the Trial Chamber has ruled and made its decision, because it is very important to note that the Trial Chamber decision does say that it is up to the Trial Chamber to rule when the reshuffling of roles would take place, so it is a decision for the Trial Chamber to make. The problem is that in this case, the Trial Chamber made this decision only for this witness, and the Trial Chamber said that at -- I don't have the exact line because I've only got the transcript with the -- but there's a specific place in the transcript where the Trial Chamber says this decision applies only to this witness. So that's the issue that I'm -- that I have trouble with this morning. So I respectfully propose two courses of action, the first one being there's an adjournment until in the real trial, in the main trial, this issue has been addressed, and then, depending on the conclusions, the Trial Chamber may respectfully decide whether to continue or not with these proceedings; or second option, I can do my application pursuant to Rule 72, and even then there would be two options: Either the Trial Chamber says it cannot rule on the motion and there's an appeal as of right to the Appeals Chamber on this issue, or the Trial Chamber does rule on the motion, and in any event, if it denies the motion, there will still be an appeal as of right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There may be a question, Mr. Bourgon, as to whether the provisions of Rule 72 applicable to an accused in relation to preliminary motions would apply in a case like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Rules apply mutatis mutandis, and it's occurring to me that there may be a question as to whether these are the kind of proceedings which are amenable to preliminary motions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In my respectful submission, Mr. President, Rule 72 does apply to this case and to this accused. Contempt proceedings before the International Tribunals, some people have argued in the past that there was no jurisdiction whatsoever for Trial Chambers to take upon -- to take on contempt proceedings. This has been made clear by the Appeals Chamber that contempt proceedings are part of the inherent powers of the Trial Chamber, and this matter is settled. The consequences of a ruling pursuant to Rule 77 can go up to seven years in detention, or imprisonment, to be more precise, or to 100.000 euros fine. Now, these are very heavy consequences which make an accused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, sorry to interrupt you. You yourself said today that you made an application for the Trial Chamber to request that these proceedings be transferred to another Chamber. That request was denied by this Chamber. Did that decision not deal with the jurisdictional issue you are raising now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe that this decision dealt with the jurisdiction issue. I believe that the jurisdiction issue at this stage is that what the Trial Chamber decided is that it would not transfer the issue to another Chamber because there was, I believe - and this is not in writing, I believe - that pursuant to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, the Trial Chamber held that there was not a reasonable apprehension of bias sufficient to transfer the case and that there was no doubt on the impartiality of the Chamber. Now, to me, Your Honour, this is completely different from the jurisdiction issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, I don't see much difference, but can I clarify one thing. When you mentioned that decision, you said that your request was denied by a majority decision. That is a misunderstanding. It was a unanimous decision. A dissenting opinion was there only as to whether to allow the adjournment or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I thank Your Honour for these precisions. Unfortunately, this is something that I did not know, and this was the purpose, if the Chamber will recall it, at the end of the hearing, when the decision was rendered to postpone until the 5th of May, I stood up and I asked the Trial Chamber, and if I remember correctly, my exact words were, "Am I to understand that this also is a decision that deals with the fact that there will not be a transfer to another Chamber?" or words to that effect. And my recollection was that the Trial Chamber then said, "Well, sort of, and there can be preliminary motions," or something like. But I don't want to bind myself into exact words, but I did raise the issue because I was very interested in knowing whether the majority decision had to do only with the postponement and also the transfer to another Trial Chamber or if it was only to one or two decisions, and I did not know this, Your Honour. So I thank you for those precisions. And with all due respect, I don't think it changes my application this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Whether that decision, Mr. President, was a majority decision or a unanimous decision, if there is a jurisdiction issue pursuant to Rule 72, there is an appeal as of right to the Appeals Chamber. Now, that's what I would like to avoid by saying why not let the main -- the parties in the main trial argue the issue of trial in absentia and the scope of what can be done by the Trial Chamber on the basis of what the Appeals Chamber said and then apply this to the contempt proceedings rather than use the contempt proceedings to raise an issue that is way beyond what is in the interest of Mr. Bulatovic but nevertheless is right to raise these issues at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, the Chamber's ruling is that it's not open to you to make a preliminary motion. In the circumstances of this case, you're disqualified to do so by virtue of Rule 72(D), and you must proceed with your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, with all due respect, I need to ask the Trial Chamber to reconsider this decision on the following basis: If we look at Rule 72(D), Mr. President, there would be -- no contempt proceedings would be justified to go under Rule 72. And I believe that the object and purpose of Rule 72 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Only on -- 72(D) is confined to jurisdiction, which is the point you take.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- if we look at 72(D), it applies to 72(A)(i), challenge jurisdiction, and also (B)(i), which takes it that someone accused of contempt could never argue the issue of jurisdiction before a Trial Chamber. Now, I respectfully submit, Mr. President and Your Honours, that barring - and I'm looking for the exact word - a person accused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Bourgon, I'm sorry that I have to interrupt you. We have given a ruling that it is not open to you in the circumstances of this case to make a preliminary motion, and we have cited the provision which precludes you from doing so, and I've indicated that you must proceed with your case for the Respondent if you have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are not reconsidering the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I will move on to the case for the Defence, and I would simply ask for a brief adjournment to meet with my client, and the object of this short adjournment is to discuss the issue of the application concerning the witness or the staff member from the Tribunal which I was not able to meet and whether I need to make this application at this time or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have two other witnesses, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, start with those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, with all due respect, they -- I understand that the Trial Chamber in this case is both prosecuting and adjudicating on the contempt proceedings, but whether I begin with my case and stop later to ask for an adjournment is a decision I should be able to make before I begin with my Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you what the Defence is?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Defence of mens rea, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But mens rea in this case is a question of whether it was done deliberately or not. If you deliberately refuse to answer a question, you have the mens rea, surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course I'm not entering into the argument stage of the case for the Defence, but it is a precedent before this own Trial Chamber, Your Honour. There is a precedent with Witness K12. And I don't know if I need to go into closed session and to discuss the issue of K12, but the issue of mens rea was discussed in those proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It appears that you are going to have an adjournment to consult with your client. May I just make one comment before you do so: There is no obligation in this Tribunal for an accused person or a respondent in a case like this to be the first witness if evidence is to be led about the case, but you may wish to consider the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. value that might be placed on the evidence, if Mr. Bulatovic is to give evidence, depending on when he gives it in relation to obviously having heard other evidence or not having heard other evidence before he gives his own account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will adjourn for ten minutes. We will be back at ten minutes to ten. --- Break taken at 9.40 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In the interests of justice, I will proceed immediately with my first witness, and I would ask, Mr. President, that following or pursuant to your advice, that I be able, after the two first witnesses, to consider my application for this other witness. I don't think I will need to make this application concerning this witness I was not able to meet, and I think it will be sufficient enough for me to hear these two witnesses. And my first witness, Mr. President, is Mr. Dragutin Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let him be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. As you --

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- have been informed, you've been called here this morning to testify in the contempt proceedings which have been initiated against a Mr. Bulatovic. For even though I have had the benefit of meeting you prior to this hearing, for the benefit of the transcript, I wish to introduce myself. My name is Stephane Bourgon and I am accompanied this morning by Ms. Jesenka Residovic, and together we represent the Respondent, Mr. Bulatovic. I have a few general questions to ask you to begin with, and I would like you to state your name, your age, and your place of birth for the benefit of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragutin Milovanovic. I was born on the 24th of August, 1957, in Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what is your occupation at the present time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm an economist graduated. At the moment I am on the labour exchange because I don't have a job.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Bulatovic, the Respondent in these proceedings; and, if so, since when have you known him and what is your relationship with Mr. Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have known Mr. Bulatovic since my childhood. We're neighbours. They're just three houses between our two houses. I grew up next to Mr. Kosta Bulatovic, and our relationship throughout since I first knew him are very good, we're very close, and for that reason I have come here to help Mr. Bulatovic here, in view of his health situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain why you are in The Hague today and why you were in The Hague last week to accompany Mr. Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Last time and this time as well, we have come here for Mr. Bulatovic to be able to present his testimony, to tell the truth as he knows it in the case against President Milosevic here. And I'm here with him, once again let me repeat the reason, for the sole reason of his poor health. Not only what you can see, that is to say that he needs a walking stick to walk with, but he has an ailing heart as well. So he cannot dress himself without help or do anything else. So I am there to help him out in every way. And we have come here and invested every effort to be before this Tribunal and to carry out our obligation, and that is for Mr. Kosta Bulatovic to tell the truth in the trial against President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. And who selected you for this assignment to accompany Mr. Bulatovic for his testimony in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Kosta Bulatovic chose me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And considering the fact that you mention being very close to Mr. Bulatovic, are you an advisor to Mr. Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. I'm not an advisor to Mr. Bulatovic. I am his personal friend, his good friend, somebody who he can be -- feel free with and act freely, and I can help him with everything he needs, all his physical needs and others, and that is the only reason that I agreed to come here with Mr. Bulatovic last time and this time too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When did you first arrive in The Hague in order to prepare for the testimony of Mr. Bulatovic before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: We arrived in The Hague for the first time on the 11th of April. It was sometime in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And during the period between the 11th of April and the day that Mr. Bulatovic was called to testify before this Trial Chamber, were you always with Mr. Bulatovic, and what exactly did you do with Mr. Bulatovic during this period?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, everywhere where I was able to go and where I had access and was allowed to be and accompany Mr. Bulatovic, which means we were in the hotel. I just wasn't with Mr. Bulatovic on two occasions that day. The day we arrived in The Hague and the following day Mr. Bulatovic was taken over by the Victims and Witness Unit, and they took him to the Scheveningen detention centre, for -- unit, for consultation and preparation with Mr. Milosevic, and I didn't have access there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that Mr. Bulatovic went to the detention centre. What was the purpose for him to go to the detention centre, and did you accompany him during those meetings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I repeat once again, I didn't accompany him to those meetings. That wasn't allowed. And the reason for his going to the Detention Unit was to prepare for his testimony with Mr. Milosevic, President Milosevic; that is, to make -- to agree upon how that was going to be conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Bulatovic, what was discussed between him and the accused Mr. Milosevic in this case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not about the details, no. Very little about that both -- on both occasions, the first time and the second time. What Mr. Bulatovic told me and what I was interested in hearing was that President Milosevic is of good health and that in his presence, while he was with the president, they took his blood pressure, and he told me that the blood pressure was very good, 140 over 90, the systolic and diastolic. So we were both very happy that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, further to these meetings between Mr. Bulatovic and Mr. Milosevic, did Mr. Bulatovic discuss with you his upcoming testimony before this Trial Chamber; and if so, what did he tell you about his testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we didn't discuss the details at all, either before his testimony or any time. The only thing he told me, and Mr. Bulatovic kept repeating this, was that he had a great desire to appear as soon as possible to be able to tell the truth as he saw it and to try and help President Milosevic in his Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you tell us a few more information concerning the health of Mr. Bulatovic, and especially the way he felt during the time preceding his testimony before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that the Trial Chamber can assess the health situation of Mr. Bulatovic itself. In 1999, Mr. Bulatovic in fact had a serious traffic accident which left him an invalid, and he is unable to walk without the aid of crutches, and it is very difficult for him to negotiate stairs without anybody -- somebody's help. However, what you can't see, what isn't visible on the outside is that Mr. Bulatovic has had several operations and that his spine has been impaired, and Mr. Bulatovic has an ailing heart, as I said, so that very often he feels numb in his legs and arms, and on one occasion I had to give him massage on his legs and arms to help with his circulation. However, Mr. Bulatovic had just one single wish, to fulfil his obligation, the obligation he made before the associates of Mr. Milosevic when they told him that the president had included him on his list of possible witnesses. So this was a duty and an honour for him, and that's how he saw it, and that's why he came here, notwithstanding his poor health, to carry out that duty. He never had a dilemma in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, as you probably know, Mr. Bulatovic testified during three days before this Trial Chamber. Where were you during the first day of his testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the first day of his testimony, I was here in the public gallery, sitting behind him, behind his back, and I was able to listen to his testimony. And when there was a break, I would leave the public gallery and go and meet him and go into the room set aside for witnesses, and that's where we would spend the break. And then when the next session started, he would come into the courtroom, and I would go to the public gallery again and listen to his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And following this first day in court, did you discuss with Mr. Bulatovic his testimony or did he discuss his testimony with you in the evening or following this testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't discuss the details because I followed it in court. What we talked about was what Mr. Bulatovic repeated all the time, and he kept asking me whether he had perhaps omitted to say something, because I, together with Mr. Bulatovic, lived in Kosovo Polje and in the general area of Kosovo and Metohija, and I know about the things that Mr. Bulatovic testified about to a considerable extent. So he just kept asking me whether I thought he had left something out that he should have said and could I make any suggestions along those lines. But I said that all the things he said were excellent but not enough; you could go on and on saying much more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, can I ask one thing. Do you follow the witness's evidence in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I don't, Your Honour. I follow it from a transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But my question is because you start to ask questions before -- while the translation is being continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I will wait. I thought that when the transcript in English was over I could start asking my questions, but I will make a longer pause. I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I take advantage of the interruption to make one thing clear from my point of view, Mr. Bourgon. If the point of this evidence is to try to establish that Mr. Bulatovic genuinely believed that the right thing to do was not to answer the questions, then you're pushing at an open door as far as I'm concerned. And what another person might have heard from him is far less demonstrative of that than what actually happened here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I take -- I take your words, Your Honour. The evidence that I intend to lead through this witness goes further than this issue, and I believe, Your Honour, that we will come to the point more important at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question to you is that whether you were present on the 19th of April during the second day of the testimony of Mr. Bulatovic and whether you saw what happened on at that day.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And following what happened in court on the 19th of April, on that day, did you have a chance to discuss what happened with Mr. Bulatovic, and did he tell you anything about his testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I had the opportunity of talking to Mr. Bulatovic. He was surprised with the extent of the lack of understanding on the part of the Trial Chamber to his conduct here. Then and now, and when he was called to come to The Hague before we actually came, when President Milosevic was first of all deprived of his right to defend himself and when there were attempts from Mr. Kay's offices or from the Tribunal to call witnesses and to ask them whether they would testify without the presence of Mr. Milosevic, at the time he clearly stated that he would not and that all he would do was to agree to come to be a witness here in the presence of Mr. Slobodan Milosevic, because he was his witness, a witness called by him. So that on that day, since President Milosevic did not appear in court, and as he followed the trial proceedings on a regular basis and that it happened on a number of occasions that Mr. Milosevic intervenes during a cross-examination and very often this has to do with interpretation, which is often corrected by Mr. Milosevic, and in view of the fact that President Milosevic has the right to intervene during the conduct of a cross-examination, he thought that he was -- he would be handicapped without Mr. Milosevic's or President Milosevic's presence, and that is why he asked that President Milosevic be present in the courtroom during his testimony so that his testimony could be of as high a level as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I follow up on that answer. You've mentioned something of some interest in general terms there. You were told that when Mr. Kay was trying to arrange evidence, the position that was presented to Mr. Bulatovic was that Mr. Milosevic would not be in court. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't say that. I -- the substance of what I wanted to say, of the core of the invitation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on. The words were "and when there were attempts from Mr. Kay's offices or from the Tribunal to call witnesses and to ask them whether they would testify without the presence of Mr. Milosevic..." Now, do you wish to change that evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can change the evidence. I don't know the details. I don't know whether that was how it was put or not. But whether he wanted to testify while being asked by Mr. Kay, and Mr. Bulatovic then, and I think now, said that he was President Milosevic's witness and would testify only if he was asked questions by the president. Is that clearer now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's clearer, but it's also different. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: To follow up on this, and which is my next question I wanted to ask you, earlier you said in response to one of my questions that Mr. Bulatovic said that he would not testify without the presence of the accused. Now, I know this might be -- look like a matter of semantics, but did he say whether that he would not testify or that he could not testify; and if so, did he qualify those words?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would like to ask the Trial Chamber and you yourself, sir, since I'm not a lawyer myself, to -- or, rather, not bring into question what I say and base it on details. I'm not very good about details and terminology, one term or another. But the substance is that on the occasion, he said that he cannot testify. He never said he didn't wish to testify. He said he could not testify without the presence of President Milosevic, because he considers it to be the basic right of every individual, including President Milosevic, if he is the accused, to be present when his case is being tried.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the -- the night of the 19th when you discussed those issues with Mr. Bulatovic, do you know whether Mr. Bulatovic had some meetings with some people? If so, do you know who these people are, and did you attend these meetings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after the first day, I think in the afternoon, a lady came to the hotel, I think, and a brief conversation took place. I was right next to them. It was in the lobby of the hotel, and several of us were present. However, it is customary when Bulatovic talks to anyone, if it has to do with his testimony, he does it on his own. I was nearby. A lady came to talk, but what they talked about I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you know whether any other people met with Mr. Bulatovic that night, and can you recall what happened and what you saw of those meetings, if any?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that that evening, after that, the legal representative of President Milosevic, Professor Rakic, came to the hotel lobby as well and that he talked to Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And were you privy to the conversation which took place between Professor Rakic and Mr. Bulatovic, and can you say anything about what was discussed between them if you were privy to that conversation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I say once again that I did not attend the conversation. It was our usual practice that Mr. Bulatovic would do this on his own. What Mr. Bulatovic said to me was, and also what particularly surprised him was that Mr. Rakic said to him that President Milosevic had wished to come here and complete these proceedings but that he was not allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you, following this meeting -- can you tell what was the attitude and the condition of Mr. Bulatovic after all these events on that night.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, in my view, was a bit perplexed concerning all of this. In his opinion, it was unnecessary. He thought then that he had come here and that his role was to assist in establishing the truth and that what he did was precisely aimed at this kind of assistance at establishing the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the next morning as you prepared for the next day in court when Mr. Bulatovic was called again on the 20th of April, did you have a chance to discuss with Mr. Bulatovic what he intended to do on the 20th of April, on that morning?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. We came to the premises here again, and until entering the courtroom, Mr. Bulatovic did not have any particular position that he wished to communicate to me. He hoped that President Milosevic would appear and that everything would be completed the way it had started.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, were you privy and where were you during his testimony on the 20th of April, and did you see what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Where I was on the first day; that is to say, in the public gallery behind Bulatovic, and I followed everything like everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber whether after the testimony of Mr. Bulatovic or after those day's events whether you had a chance to discuss with Mr. Bulatovic what had happened and whether he told you anything about his testimony.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I repeat once again, we did not discuss the details of his testimony as I followed it and I was aware of it. He had no dilemma in terms of completing his testimony. He was just perplexed because the conditions had been changed in relation to the first day when he had started and when he had completed the first part of his evidence in the presence of Mr. Milosevic. Then Mr. Nice completed part of the cross-examination too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, considering that you are somewhat close to Mr. Bulatovic, can you say whether those day's events had an impact on his physical condition and his emotional condition?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is certain that such events would affect even the healthiest of people, let alone a person in Mr. Bulatovic's health condition. All of this affected him, and he was rather exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And during those -- the time you spent with him after the trial, did Mr. Bulatovic express any anger towards the Tribunal or any other observations in respect of his testimony that you could share with the Trial Chamber this morning?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I can say here with full responsibility that he did not display any anger, only hope. At every moment, Mr. Bulatovic had the hope that it would continue the following day. He expected that the Trial Chamber would understand. He thought that it was at one moment that the Trial Chamber acted hastily, and he wanted to contribute to establishing the truth, and he thought that this was would be taken into account, that the trial would continue and that we would finish what we had come here to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. When were you supposed to go back to your home at that time, and what happened exactly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of the second day, the service that accompanies us here - and we are not allowed to move about without them anyway - they told us that we would be travelling to Belgrade the following day. We prepared our luggage, and we informed our families that they should be waiting for us the following day as we were due to arrive in Belgrade the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the Trial Chamber knows, of course, as well as you do that those plans changed at that time, but can you describe how it came about that those travel plans were changed.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: We do not know how that came about. A lady from the Victims and Witness Unit - and they accompanied us throughout our stay here, and I can only give them every credit for their professionalism - this lady came in the evening and said that things had changed, that we would be staying on until Monday and that on Monday Mr. Bulatovic's testimony would continue, that Mr. Milosevic's health had improved and that on Monday he would be testifying in the presence of President Milosevic. So we called our families and we said that we would be staying on for a while longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I apologise for the interpreters. I did not see the end of the last question. What you mentioned just at the end of your last answer, what I would like to know is whether Mr. Bulatovic was asked whether he wanted to testify or whether he was told he was going to testify on Monday.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: They did not ask him whether he wanted to testify, they simply informed him that he would be staying on and that as of Monday he would continue his testimony in the presence of President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how did Mr. Bulatovic react to the fact that he was told that he would testify on Monday?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the lady who informed Mr. Bulatovic of this can confirm this: Mr. Bulatovic crossed himself, which is rather characteristic of him, and he said thank goodness that this would happen. That is to say that he could hardly wait for it to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In case you're concerned about the mystery, Mr. Bourgon, when I learned on the Friday that arrangements were being made for Mr. Bulatovic to return, and I also learned that Mr. Milosevic was likely to be in court on the Monday, it was I who suggested to the court liaison officer that consideration might be given to Mr. Bulatovic's evidence being completed on the Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I knew that there had been somewhat an involvement from a liaison officer, but I did not know the details as to how that came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question is simply based on the fact and your previous answers where you said that you know Mr. Bulatovic since you were a young man, can you qualify how well you know Mr. Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that I know him quite well. As much as a child can know his parent, or to put it in milder terms, as they say in our part of the world, I know him as a nephew could know him, or a cousin. I grew up next to Kosta Bulatovic. He was president of the football club where I played football, and we would see each other practically every day in our house or Kosta Bulatovic's house until things happened the way they did and Kosta went on to Pristina. He moved there, but we still consider ourselves to be family.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My last question is as follows: You mentioned that you arrived in The Hague in the company of Mr. Bulatovic on the 11th of April, and according to the fact that he testified on the 25th, I take it that you probably returned home either on that day or the next day, meaning that you spent some 15 days in The Hague with Mr. Bulatovic. Now, my question is as follows: During all this time and everything that happened, would you say that at any time Mr. Bulatovic gave you the impression that it was his aim to interfere in the administration or of justice and with this trial?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, we came on the 11th and we returned on the 26th to Belgrade. I claim with full responsibility that throughout that time and after arriving in Belgrade, Kosta Bulatovic had only one wish, and that was to complete his testimony, for it to be of the highest quality possible, and as he says, to pay his debt to the truth and to justice. That prevailed over the past several days, too. Had it not been for that, we would not have been here yesterday either in view of the circumstances involved, so that people would not think that Kosta did not want to come here and testify here. This time we went at our own initiative over the holidays to the Dutch embassy, but there were holidays and they weren't working. And then after that, we went back to the Dutch embassy after the holiday and then they sent us to the ICTY office, and Ms. Milenov can confirm all of that. Until that moment, we had not received any information as to when we were supposed to come except for what was told on that day here. Who would give us visas, how we would come, on which plane, we didn't know any of that. At that moment when we went there at our own initiative, this young lady started the mechanism going, and she can confirm that that is how we came here, how we got visas, how we booked flights. And that speaks in itself that Mr. Bulatovic's only interest was to do what he had come here to do, and that is to say -- to prove what was true in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. interest of justice, and he tried to do it in the best possible way. I think that it is absurd in view of his behaviour and in view of his health condition to have any thoughts of him having had any kind of ill intention. He only thought what I had explained just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I have no more questions, but the Honourable Judges from this Trial Chamber may have some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have no questions of you, Mr. Milovanovic. Thank you for testifying here, and you may now leave. In any event, we'll now take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My next witness is Professor Branko Rakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RAKIC
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You are called this morning to testify in the proceedings against the Respondent, and that is the contempt proceedings. My first question would be to -- could you please state your name, your age, and your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RAKIC
utterances.text: My name is Branko Rakic. I was born in 1961 in Ivanica, Serbia. At that time it was Yugoslavia, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what is your present occupation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RAKIC
utterances.text: I teach at the law school of Belgrade University. At the same time, I'm present here as legal advisor to Mr. Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, your testimony, Professor, should be relatively focussed considering that the Trial Chamber already knows that on the night of the 19th of April, you met with Mr. Bulatovic, and I would like you to first begin by saying how and for what reason was this meeting organised on the night of the 19th of April.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RAKIC
utterances.text: Well, on the 19th of April, in the afternoon, Ms. Evelyn Anoya, who is the liaison officer between the Defence and the Trial Chamber, called me concerned because of the overall situation since the witness refused to testify under changed circumstances. She thought that the witness should have greater confidence in us from the Defence team, who had had contact with him before, than in others, because as far as I know, another lawyer had talked to him before that. She asked me to talk to him to tell him what the situation was and to see whether he would be prepared to perhaps review his decision. I said that I personally was ready to do that, but there were two constraints. One is the fact that the witness had already started giving evidence, and I do not have the right to contact witnesses who had already started giving evidence. Secondly, I had to have the consent of President Milosevic. And she said that she would see with the Trial Chamber that this restriction be lifted, that is to say that we could discuss only the new situation, not his evidence itself. And also, she said that she would get in touch with Professor -- President Milosevic so that he could call me from the Detention Unit, because there is no other way for me to get in touch with him, so that he would give me his consent. Also, Evelyn Anoya called me and told me that I could see the witness, that there would be no ban on seeing the witness altogether. Of course, we could only discuss the new situation. And also, President Milosevic telephoned me after that and said that he agreed to my talking to Mr. Bulatovic. He also said that he had asked to come himself the following day and in this way redress the situation, but he was told that he would not be allowed to go in view of his continuing high blood pressure. So then I went to see him. I don't know exactly what time it was, but I went somewhere in the early evening to talk to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Considering, Professor, that those two constraints that you've mentioned had been lifted, did you in fact meet with Mr. Bulatovic? Where did the meeting take place, and can you describe and give an account of what was discussed during that meeting.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RAKIC
utterances.text: Well, we met at the hotel lobby. The Bilderberg Europa Hotel in Scheveningen, where Mr. Bulatovic was staying anyway. Practically, we talked on our own, but Mr. Milovanovic, who was accompanying him, was very close to us, and at some of the other tables there were some other witness who -- witnesses who were there before they came to court to give evidence. I presented the situation to him from a legal and factual point of view. Actually, first of all when I approached him, he looked at me with this expression, sort of what's going on? What is this? And then I tried to explain to him that he was in a situation that is legally covered by Rule 77 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, that these were actually proceedings that have to do with the obstruction of justice. He reacted to that. He said, "I testified. I gave evidence." His reaction was that this had sort of hurt him, the very use of these words, "obstruction of justice." He said, "Well, I've already testified for a while, and I showed all due respect to the Trial Chamber and the Prosecutor, who was unpleasant towards me. I treated him very courteously too. I came here to contribute to justice rather than obstruct it." He said that he believed that it is more just if he continues to testify in the presence of Mr. Milosevic, because he said, "After all, Mr. Milosevic is the one who called me to testify here. With all due respect to everyone else, I think his presence is indispensable." He also mentioned that out of all the persons sitting in the courtroom, he had only conducted preparations with Mr. Milosevic. He's the only person that he had talked to in advance. In hindsight now, I said two things that perhaps had an effect on him. Now, I mean viewed in hindsight. At that time, it didn't cross my mind. One thing was that I mentioned that Mr. Milosevic, though ill, wanted to come the following day. The reaction was, I think -- I mean this is what I infer, I cannot say this with 100 per cent certainty -- Mr. Bulatovic was a bit taken aback. Like, he was ill and nevertheless prepared to come to the courtroom, even though ill, in order to prevent this kind of thing from happening, and it would only be fair for me not to testify in his absence. He didn't say these words, but his gesticulations seemed to suggest that. The second thing I wish to say, in hindsight now and which perhaps affected his confirming his original decision, this was just a routine legal question that was put at the time, when he mentioned to me that no one would be present in the courtroom who had prepared him to testify, who would be questioning me, he said. And I said, "Well, Steven Kay." And he said, "Well, I've never seen him. I never spoke to him. I only know him from the courtroom. Do I have the right to talk to Steven Kay at all?" And then I told him something which was a technical matter although perhaps I should have consulted before that, and I said, "Well, you do not have the right to see anyone from the Defence since you've already started giving evidence." I don't know whether that perhaps affected his decision and perhaps contributed to all of this now that I think about it. But his attitude was, "I want to testify, but I cannot now that Milosevic is not here. I don't think I'm obstructing justice. On the contrary, I want to contribute to justice. And the truth." And the truth. Perhaps the truth even ranked first in terms of everything that he wanted to get across.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What did you gather he meant when he said he cannot, he wants to testify but he cannot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously what happened later on, as far as I understand things; that he wanted to testify but that he thought that he would damage President Milosevic in some way if he testified in his absence, that that was the core of the matter. And that in this way he would not contribute to what he had come here for, and that is the truth. He believes that the truth works in favour of Mr. Milosevic and, therefore, in his absence he did not wish to have anything happen that would work to his detriment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I just have one last question, Professor, and that is as part of those discussions, did the issue of interpretation and the role played by Mr. Milosevic in this respect, according to the accused, was that discussed with you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RAKIC
utterances.text: Well, this description of the problems in case Mr. Milosevic is absent is one of the central issues. I cannot give you all the details, but I can give you the gist of it. He mentioned who would now be on the side of the Defence in his absence, and one of the things was, yes, that Mr. Milosevic intervened from time to time in case there are any omissions in the interpretation or other omissions that he can note. It is a fact that not only during his testimony but in Serbia and Montenegro Mr. Milosevic's trial is viewed widely, so people know about the trial and what goes on here. At least, they see it from the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I just have one final question for you, and that is did you see your role when you had this discussion with Mr. Bulatovic as that of a legal advisor or whether this was not the point? What exactly was your role when you went to see him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RAKIC
utterances.text: I was not the one who set my role. I was actually asked by Ms. Evelyn Anoya to try to talk to him and to put the facts to him and to see whether he was ready to -- well, perhaps I was a person he would trust more than a lawyer who he'd see for the first time. And I think that before that he saw a lady, I think her name was Jelena Nikolic. So what I said was of legal substance, too, but I don't think that that really mattered. I was supposed to see what his position was and how firm it was and whether he'd be willing to change it. At the end, when Mr. Bulatovic was supposed to come back, Ms. Anoya called me and said that she talked to Judge Bonomy and that he said that these two proceedings, that is to say proceedings according to Rule 77 and the proceedings against President Milosevic were two separate proceedings and that therefore there was no problem in terms of the testimony continuing. She mentioned Monday, and since I was there with the other witnesses at the hotel, I know I saw Mr. Bulatovic. I could not discuss this any further, but in the meantime, I was in contact with him, talked to him. He was rather depressed, but then he felt better, much better, because his feeling was that he was going back with business unfinished. Despite the risk involved in this -- in these proceedings, he was greatly bolstered by the fact that he would carry out his duty to tell the truth. I am simply saying that what I saw after that was that he was a completely different person, feeling completely different, in a different mood.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor. I have no further questions. Maybe the Honourable Judges have some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No questions. Thank you, Professor Branko Rakic, for testifying. You may leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good-bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, considering that -- that witness was before the Chamber on the 19th and the 20th of April and that he had the chance to explain his position and that he did so to a great extent, answering the questions of the Judges, and that on the 25th he completed his testimony, as the Trial Chamber knows, and that he also made a statement at the end, in the interests of justice, for the sake of saving the precious time of this Trial Chamber, Mr. Bulatovic will not testify in his own defence today and I'm ready to address the Chamber and to make my final arguments when the Trial Chamber is ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I therefore confirm that the Defence rests, and I now provide the Trial Chamber with my submissions concerning the contempt proceedings which have been initiated against Mr. Bulatovic. The first thing I would like to do, Mr. President, is to of course go over the charge itself. And the charge itself was read by the Trial Chamber at the beginning, and in terms of the charge, it says that on the 19th and the 20th of April, being a witness before Trial Chamber III, he knowingly and wilfully interfered with the administration of justice by contumaciously refusing to answer questions asked by the Prosecution. Mr. President, there are, of course, essential elements to this charge, and these essential elements include the fact that he refused to answer questions asked by the Prosecution, and I think that the evidence is on the record, and I will not get -- provide any arguments with respect to this essential element. However, Mr. President, the other element is the fact that he was a witness before Trial Chamber III is also, of course, undisputed. What is at issue here is whether the other essential ingredient is fulfilled, and that is he knowingly and wilfully interfered with the administration of justice, and by contumaciously refusing to answer questions asked by the Prosecution. Mr. President, the mens rea requirement under this charge, I respectfully submit, is that the witness must knowingly and wilfully interfere with the administration of justice. That means that there must be actual knowledge from the witness that he is indeed interfering with the administration of justice. In this respect, it is important to note --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Might it not also be inferred from the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, my submission, Mr. President, will be that it must be actual knowledge, and I will get to that and explain where -- what I propose as the foundation for this requirement that it must be actual knowledge that he is interfering with the administration of justice. And of course not only the actual knowledge but he is -- actually wants, wilfully wants to interfere with the administration of justice. In this respect, I will start by looking at the issue of Witness K12 before this Trial Chamber. In the issue of Witness K12, by majority decision, the Trial Chamber held that "contumacious" had to be given the interpretation of or the sense of perverse, and the Trial Chamber found that Witness K12 or -- vacated the finding of contempt of court because it was not established that the contempt in itself was contumacious in the sense of being perverse. The facts in this case is that Witness K12 was a witness for the Prosecution. Now, what happened is that he refused to answer questions, apparently for security reasons. It is not clear, but it appears from a reading of that transcript that he would have refused to testify in the presence of the accused, or at least that this was his motivation. The proceedings were adjourned for the Prosecution until the day after, and the Prosecution was invited -- sorry, the Prosecution actually invited the Chamber to exercise its powers against the witness manifestly hostile and who did not consider -- the Prosecution, sorry, did not consider the reason given by the witness to refuse to testify as sufficient. The Trial Chamber gave a preliminary ruling of contempt on the 4th of June, and adjourned the matter for 20 days. In the end, as I've mentioned, it was determined that the refusal of the witness was not contumacious. Now, there was a dissent with this opinion, with this ruling, a dissent by the Honourable Judge Kwon, who said that in his view, contumacious was not an additional ingredient but was actually part of Rule 77 in the sense of interference with the administration of justice knowingly and wilfully. And Honourable Judge Kwon mentioned that contumacious element sets a high threshold, or too high of a threshold to make a finding. According to his interpretation, "knowingly, wilfully, contumaciously" should be interpreted as meaning an obstinate refusal to answer without a reasonable excuse. And Judge Kwon was of the view that K12, by refusing to answer questions of the Prosecution for security reasons, apparently, were not reasonable. Now, of course I recall, Mr. President, that this was the dissent and that the majority view of the Trial Chamber was that refusing to testify for security reason was in fact not a contumacious. Looking at the jurisprudence of this Tribunal where we found that the issue of the mens rea requirement was basically explained by the Appeals Chamber. I refer to the case of the Prosecutor versus Aleksovski, and that is the case International Tribunal 95-14/1-AR-R77. In this case, the Appeals Chamber held that to be held in contempt of the Tribunal, it must be established that the Respondent acted with specific intent with the Tribunal's administration of justice. This was also established in the Prosecutor versus Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Bourgon. Could you repeat that. Must be established that the Respondent acted ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: With specific intent to interfere with the Tribunal's administration of justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Just the words "to interfere" were missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this specific quote, Your Honour, comes from the Prosecutor versus Brdjanin, case number International Tribunal 99-36-R77, decision on motion for acquittal, on the 19th of March, 2004. The Appeals Chamber has defined this specific intent as actual knowledge. Illustrations of actual knowledge of contempt include the following: A deliberate publication of material presenting a real risk of prejudice to the fair trial of an accused where the act of publication may have occurred even in ignorance of existence of the trial. A second example: A deliberate publication of material with knowledge of the existence of the trial and either with the specific intent -- intention, sorry, of influencing its result or where that material would have the effect of influencing its result. Another illustration given is the publication of a witness identity where protective measures have been granted to avoid such disclosure, again with knowledge of the existence of those measures and with the specific intention of frustrating their effect, where the contempt is based not upon the violation of the order granted -- granting, sorry, protective measures but because the disclosure interfered with the administration of justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The contempt in that case was the disclosure of measures that had been protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President, and that's why, of course, these are illustrations. But they do show, and they do illustrate what is meant by the specific intent requirement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the second one you gave, Brdjanin, applies even in ignorance of the trial. Does it not follow from that that what matters is the deliberate act of publicising the material?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, the second example I gave Your Honour talks about the specific intention of influencing its result or where the material would have the effect of influencing its result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Even in ignorance of the existence of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, even in the existence -- of course, that means we're talking about the material presented a real risk of prejudice. So all these examples highlight the specific intent in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But are you understanding the point that that applies even where the person publicising the material does not know that there is a trial? That's surely a low standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Your Honour, when the person does not know where there is a trial but nevertheless that person, according to this illustration, has published material that has a real risk of prejudice to the fair trial of an accused. Now, what is meant here by not knowing about the existence of the trial does not refer to the fact that we don't know a trial is going on. It might be that not knowledge whether the trial is on or finished or terminated or yet to begin, but the specific intent is that there's a real risk and there is an awareness of that real risk. Now, the fourth example or illustration given by -- in this case was wilful blindness. And wilful blindness, I take it, is something that the Trial Chamber is quite familiar with. Now, when we look at this specific intent requirement, it is important to look at what happened in this case. And in this case, you have a witness who comes before the Trial Chamber, and you have ample evidence that he wanted to testify, that there was no holding back on his testimony, and that he started to testify, and that he treated everyone in the courtroom with respect, and that he was responding to the questions. Now, that is the questions of the accused Mr. Milosevic in his capacity as his own counsel, some questions of the Trial Chamber, as well as the questions of the Prosecution. The witness, according to the information or the evidence available to the Trial Chamber, has seen on TV and has experienced for himself - that is on the record also - that Mr. Milosevic did interfere at some places and did play a role --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Intervene. Thank you very much, Mr. President. Intervene to make some comments with respect to the interpretation and the translation of some words, and that was of assistance to the witness. Some days go by before the witness appears again before the Trial Chamber, and when the witness comes back to testify, no one has warned him that Mr. Milosevic will not be there. By the time he appears in court, he finds out that Mr. Milosevic is not there. For him, that creates a problem, and he expresses his views that he cannot continue, and he tries to explain why. Now, of course, the witness is not a lawyer, and the words he may have used might not have been clear to the Trial Chamber in terms of the reasons he was saying that he could not testify. What is sure, however, and what evidence the Trial Chamber does have is that he knew that an accused has the right to be present at his trial. So for him, that's the first problem.
