The second problem is Mr. Milosevic in this case is not only the accused, he is also the counsel examining the witness. So in the witness's mind, I respectfully put it to you, Your Honours, that there are two people missing that day. Not only is the accused missing but the person conducting the examination is missing. And the witness knows that after counsel for the Prosecution will be done with his cross-examination, there's supposed to be questions asked of him by Mr. Milosevic, and Mr. Milosevic is not there. He did express the situation with Professor Rakic, and he said, "Well, can I see Mr. Kay before?" And the answer was no. So he's left to himself. It's not that he wants, and there is no indication whatsoever that he wants to interfere with justice, but he has a problem. Mr. Milosevic will not be there to correct the interpretation, that goes for both the cross-examination and the re-examination, and he doesn't know who will be asking the re-examination. In this respect, it is important to look at the prejudice in the witness's mind that goes both to him and to the accused. It is a well-known fact that when two persons in a common-law setting prepare a testimony, they will discuss how questions will be asked and they will discuss, sometimes even adopt, some kind of strategy, or a counsel may inform, and I say may inform, the witness of his strategy. It may be that -- and we don't know this, but it may be that the witness knows that certain questions will be asked of him during cross-examination, and therefore these questions can no longer be asked. And the witness, what we know on the evidence in this case, he expressed to Professor Rakic, that he's scared to damage the case of Mr. Milosevic. He came here to give the truth, he came here to participate in this trial, to fulfil his duty before an International Tribunal, and then he says all this has changed and I may actually have the opposite effect. Can we, on the basis of what happened on the 25th of April, look at what actually happened during the cross-examination, because as the Prosecution counsel put it to the Trial Chamber before the order of contempt was issued, counsel for the Prosecution said it is time for court-assigned counsel to play their role. There are videos. There is a camera. There is no prejudice. And in addition, we can always recall the witness later if there is a problem. Well, immediately one may think if we are going to recall the witness later anyway, what is the purpose of pressing on, to use the words of the Prosecution, on that very day? But when we look at what happened Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. during the re-examination of Mr. Milosevic on Monday, the 25th of April, we fully realise that court assigned counsel could not have performed that re-examination in the same way that Mr. Milosevic did it. And I offer to this Trial Chamber two examples. The first example is the transcript of 25th April. And that was on page 38696 where, re-examined by Mr. Milosevic, the issue of Siptar as an offending word to Albanians is raised by Mr. Milosevic, and the question is: "Did you ever hear anyone insulting Albanians when they called them Siptars?" Sorry for my pronunciation if my pronunciation is wrong. But then -- of course that question could have been put by anyone. But then adding the fact that the following question at lines 22 to 25: "Do you know that in the public gallery they have different channels in terms of how they can listen to different languages?" And that channel 3 refers to "Shqip" or "Sip," which is the Albanian language on that list of languages. This kind of knowledge, despite all the research, is not the kind of things that could come handily to court assigned counsel, and it shows that it was important in this respect for the accused himself to continue with the cross-examination. The second example I wish to raise is on page 38710, and that is the issue of the poem. The question put by Mr. Milosevic in re-examination, where we see: "Very well. Mr. Nice asked you why you react emotionally to the death of the Turkish Tzar Murat." Now, I don't read all of the questions, but what is important is that on page 38711, Mr. Milosevic says on this video, "You are quoting folklore here -- there. It is an epic poem that you are in fact quoting." And the Chamber even put the question, "Was the journalist made aware that you were quoting from this epic poem?" Now this, in my view, Mr. President, shows that the Trial Chamber was interested in the evidence which was attempted by the Prosecution during its cross-examination by showing a small part of a video which basically, to use common language, blew in his face. But would court counsel have been able to know that this was the epic poem, especially at this point in time? Now, this is the type of discussions that may have taken place between the accused and the Respondent when he informed him of what questions he was going to ask. And now the witness feels that those type of questions, he will not be able to correct that situation and to do justice to the party who called him, and whether we agree or not with whose party he came on the behalf of, it is clear from the record that telling the truth for this witness was telling the truth in favour of Mr. Milosevic. Now, whether we like this or not, whether we agree or not, is not an important question at this stage. At this stage is, did the witness have a reasonable excuse for saying, "I want to testify, but I cannot unless Mr. Milosevic is there. He started it, and I'll come back at any time to finish it." And he did say this to the Trial Chamber. And when given an opportunity to come back and to finish the work --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If he has what you say is a reasonable excuse, in your submission he cannot have knowingly and wilfully interfered with the administration of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This in some respect is my submission, Mr. President, that the specific intent would be where the witness does something and he knows that he is interfering with the administration of justice. And we are not talking about a lawyer. We are talking about an honest citizen. We're talking of a man, a sick man, a man who is old, and a man who is, according to the evidence in these proceedings, came here to do good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're also saying that if he -- if he had an honest belief that what he was doing was right, he cannot have knowingly and wilfully interfered with the administration of justice and his conduct would not have been contumacious.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the words "honest belief" that you mentioned now, I did not mention these words of "honest belief," and I hesitate to go down that read. I don't want to say what is an example of what could not be contumacious. I want to say that what the actual conduct of the Respondent here shows that he did not have this intent. He did not know, and did he not wilfully interfere in the administration of justice, because, for him, he was doing good, and he thought that answering these questions would damage his testimony. The Trial Chamber did raise the issue what is more important. Is it more important for a witness who will come and has not begun to testify yet or for a witness who is in the middle of his testimony? I submit respectfully, Mr. President, that the prejudice and the reasons on the witness not to answer a question are much greater when he is in the middle of the testimony, because there is a change of circumstance. And what I was saying a few minutes ago is as soon as he was given an opportunity to come back and to finish his testimony, despite his medical condition, of which you have now ample evidence, he did not hesitate a minute. He was told, "You're going to testify on Monday." His reaction, "Thank God. I did not want to leave with unfinished business." Now, if we also look at what he said on the 25th of April just before leaving, and he basically addressed the Trial Chamber with the leave of the President, and he said the following: He basically said that he came here as a Defence witness with the best of intention. It never even occurred to him that there were any problems. In the presence of Milosevic he answered all questions, and he believes that he expresses respect to all of the parties. And then he says at lines 8 to 10 on page 38720, "...in the absence of ... Mr. Milosevic, therefore, in totally -- under totally new circumstances, I could not continue testifying. "... my intention was not to obstruct or slow down in any way the proceedings. On the contrary, my intention from the very beginning was and remains to contribute to establishing of truth and insist in the administration of justice in fair -- in a fair situation." And he said, "I fulfil my obligation," and "I go home with a completely clear conscience." And he said, "I would like to thank you," and on and on. That is the intention, Mr. President, expressed by the witness. This is what he's feeling in terms of his contribution to this trial. He did his duty, he's happy that he's given the opportunity to finish his testimony, and he has a clear conscience, and he says thank you to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, you referred to the Chamber's decision in K12 and that the Chamber interpreted "contumaciously" as meaning perversely, but you didn't develop any submissions on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have here the transcript of what happened in the decision in Witness K12, but just to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I want to hear is how you apply that to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, in my -- in my view, Mr. President, when we talk about perverse and the way it was used by the Honourable Presiding Judge at the time, was perverse in the sense of there was some bad intention. He knew that he was doing something not only wrong objectively but wrong to the justice, wrong to what he was participating in -- participating in. That's the meaning of "perverse," in my view. And in my respectful submission, even going with the criteria developed by the Honourable Judge Kwon in his dissenting opinion, having a reasonable excuse, or taking the majority view of perverse, in both cases the evidence in these proceedings show that this was never -- there is no evidence that the witness ever wanted to have this intent of wilfully and knowing -- and knowingly interfering. He did say to the Trial Chamber, and that's on the record, "I'll come back at any time to finish my testimony. Please allow me to do so."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have you taken account of the fact that it was explained to the witness that he was obliged to testify, that safeguards had been put in place to ensure that there would be no prejudice to Mr. Milosevic? Mr. Milosevic would have the benefit of a video, a videotape of the proceedings and the transcript, and that it would have been open to Mr. Milosevic to recall the witness. What is your submission in the light of all of that in relation to the question of the mens rea?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, indeed I did address that issue earlier when I was speaking about how the witness felt about continuing to testify and the damage he could do to the case. In fact, it's on the record the Trial Chamber tried to reassure the witness. However, it's important to note that the Trial Chamber, in reassuring the witness on the 20th, did say and -- did say that what was happening was there was a number of possibilities which could take place, and I would just like to quote where the Trial Chamber said -- Trial Chamber said -- sorry. When informing the witness of the situation, and the Trial Chamber did inform him, "You will need to be advised carefully, because if you maintain your position, it must be clear that you're liable to be charged." But the Trial Chamber also said, "It is also very possible that the Trial Chamber will totally ignore the evidence that you have given. That is to say the Chamber will attach no weight to it at all." Now, that, Mr. President, is kind of a -- what was told to the witness. He wasn't given basically the word, "If you don't answer, you will be in contempt." You said, "You're liable to be found in contempt." In my respectful submission, that was an invitation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is wrong with that? It's the correct thing to say, that you're liable to be charged with contempt.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's perfectly -- I would never say that this was not proper for the Trial Chamber to say that. What I'm saying, Mr. President, is what effect did these words have on a non-lawyer even though he was later on to receive legal advice? Because to him it may have been options: Maybe contempt, maybe it is the situation of having the evidence stricken from the record. But I don't believe that these -- the information that was given to him make it so that he inevitably understood and knew that he was interfering with the administration of justice. Did he understand that there was a problem? That could be, but we cannot tell from the evidence on the record whether he thought that this was actually a problem. Now, a very important aspect that I wish to highlight is the attitude of the Prosecution, because this can help us to identify whether there was a wilful interference, because the Prosecution did, when it invited the Trial Chamber to exercise its powers of contempt, did highlight a couple of examples. For example, counsel for the Prosecution said, "I wonder how come this witness comes in the courtroom this morning and he knows exactly how much time I have left." Now, that was a direct suggestion, or an implicit suggestion at the least, that there was some understanding that the witness wanted to do something bad to the trial because he must have been -- must have had some understanding or some agreement with somebody else, whether the accused or another person, not to answer questions. That's what the counsel for the Prosecution was saying. And then counsel for the Prosecution later on referred to a second example, and counsel for the Prosecution said that this was blatant disregard and that this was wrong and that this was -- had to be -- had to be -- I'm looking for the exact words. "... he declines to be cross-examined. The evidence should be struck altogether, and it should stand at naught, and he should then be dealt with forthwith for contempt. Testimony be a disasterous precedent to allow witnesses to attempt to control the Court like this." So Mr. Nice, counsel for the Prosecution, gave examples of what could be wilfully and knowingly interfering with the administration of justice. The person comes here with the intent of doing something wrong or stopping his testimony. Or the witness comes here and he has the intent to do something or to kind of control the agenda of the Court. Now, the distress of the Prosecution in this case can be understood. This has been a long trial. I'm not part of the trial, but I know, like most people, that this is a long trial, and the Prosecution is distressed by the fact that this is what it says would be an example of the accused trying to control the agenda of the Court. If there was evidence of such nature, maybe, Mr. President, the Court could go the way of wilfully and knowingly interfering with the administration of justice. But in this case, with all the evidence we have, with everything that was said by the two witnesses today, everything that was said by the witness on the record, we have no evidence whatsoever that there was this wilful and knowingly interfering. I'd like to refer quickly to another case before this Tribunal, but for this purpose I need to go into closed session, with your leave, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Closed or private?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Private session, sorry. "Huis clos partiel," sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was saying, Mr. Bourgon, to my mind -- I was saying that to my mind, that case doesn't help you at all because contempt proceedings were not considered there. So how does it help?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The issues we're considering here did not arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In my submission, Mr. President, this is case is of assistance to this Trial Chamber because there was a situation, there was a witness who refused to testify, and for some reason this witness was -- no proceedings were instituted, in all likelihood because the excuse and the reasons given by the witness were considered that it did not warrant contempt proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're now in the realm of speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In this case -- well, we have the facts, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, was that witness brought before the Court and asked to take the declaration and give evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did he refuse at that stage in court?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And was he then ordered to give evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Pardon me, Your Honour? I missed the last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was he then ordered to give evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have the transcript with me and I cannot confirm whether he was ordered. He was asked whether he wanted to testify and he said no, twice, and twice he was sent back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And these questions were asked in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I raise this for two things: As an example of a reasonable excuse, but also as to ensure that we don't adopt a double standard before the International Tribunal. Mr. President, I think that at this time, I will close my argument by simply saying that everything you've heard, whether it is today or the 19th and the 20th of April, and on the 25th of April when the witness had the first opportunity, accepted to complete his testimony, such a witness, in my view, based on the evidence, surely did not knowingly and wilfully interfere with the administration of justice. What really happened that week? Was there an interference with justice? Well, sure, there was a delay in the justice. But was the delay caused by this witness, or was the delay caused by the fact that the accused did not show up because he could not show up? I think that is a very important consideration as to whether what was reason. And the Court will also recall that when court assigned counsel was asked whether he could proceed with the next witness, to my recollection, and I'm not sure completely of what I'm saying, but the court assigned counsel was not able to proceed with the next witness. The week -- that week of hearing would have been lost in any event. Is this witness responsible for that down time? Everyone one understands, Mr. President -- when I say everyone, it's the international community understands what is going on before this Trial Chamber and the pressure that is on every party in the courtroom to complete a very important trial. But the evidence that you have before you, is it that this witness, has he been in contempt of court by his actions? I wish to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'd like to say, Mr. Bourgon, that the Chamber is not affected in anything that it does, in any decision that it takes in the Milosevic case, by any kind of pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise if this is the impression of what I said. I referred to parties, and of course far from my intention to say that the Trial Chamber reacted to pressures. This would be absolutely inappropriate for me to even suggest that. What I say, Mr. President, is that the parties in this case, and that is whether it is the accused and the Prosecution, there is immense pressure as to what is going on in the courtroom. And as a Defence counsel before this Tribunal, I fully trust that this is not a thing that -- the Trial Chambers are not under such pressure, and I really apologise if this is the impression I gave the Trial Chamber. I would simply like to raise a last argument, and that was taken from Archbold, which I believe the Court is quite familiar with, and I don't -- this is on chapter 28, 126, where we discuss the sentencing of persons found in contempt, and one of the issues is someone may be found in contempt, and the suggestion that is made is that sentencing should wait because that person might, in the end, fulfil his or her duty and testify. So I'm not highlighting this issue to tell you that there should be any sentencing in this case, because I firmly believe and it is my respectful submission that there was no contempt on the part of this witness, but this shows that the fact that the witness came back at the earliest opportunity is a sign, is a repair of this time that maybe was lost in the eyes of the Trial Chamber. For all these reasons, Your Honours, I respectfully submit that Mr. Kosta Bulatovic did not commit contempt on the 19th and the 20th of April, 2005, because he never wilfully and knowingly interfered with the administration of justice. And I'm not sure what the exact language should be, whether I should seek for an acquittal or, as in the case of Witness K12, that the initial findings of contempt be vacated. In any event, there was no contempt on behalf of Mr. Kosta Bulatovic. He has shown that he is an honourable man. He has come back here for his contempt proceedings. He trusts this Tribunal. He has expressed respect for this Tribunal. He should be allowed to go home. And I think that everyone has taken the point well on board as to what should take place, what are the responsibilities of witnesses in any criminal trial. Respectfully submitted, I'm grateful, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider this matter and give its decision on Friday of next week, and the Respondent will be advised prior to that time whether he should return. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.
